body.text: As part of his Europe tour, Mongolia’s President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa made a state visit to Finland from October 22-24. As Mongolia and Finland will be celebrating the 65th anniversary of their diplomatic relationship in 2028, Khurelsukh’s state visit to Helsinki demonstrate a political will on both sides to strengthen bilateral relations and seek active cooperation mechanisms.

On October 23, Khurelsukh arrived in Helsinki for a state visit at the invitation of Finnish President Alexander Stubb. Khurelsukh’s visit to Helsinki marks a diplomatic milestone as it was the first visit by a Mongolian head of state to Finland in 16 years. Mongolia’s then-President Elbegdorj Tsakhia paid a visit to Finland in 2010.

During the summit, Stubb welcomed the Mongolian delegation by saying “Finland and Mongolia have a lot in common. We both value democracy and stability. We are both small countries bordering larger neighbors and we are committed supporters of the multilateral system and the United Nations.”

Khurelsukh’s state visit to Finland creates a path for Ulaanbaatar and Helsinki to strengthen bilateral relations. It also highlights a broader trend: more and more small states are seeking to upgrade their cooperation mechanisms as a way of navigating a rapidly changing geopolitical environment.

Mongolia and Finland established official diplomatic relations in 1963. Two years earlier, in 1961, Finland supported Mongolia’s admission to the United Nations. Since then, both Finland and Mongolia have become avid supporters and participants in the global multilateral systems, including the U.N., Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), World Trade Organization (WTO), and International Monetary Fund (IMF). Ulaanbaatar and Helsinki share track records of strong voting alignment on global issues such as governance, human rights, international law, and climate change.

In December 2024, Mikko Kinnunen was appointed as non-resident ambassador of Finland to Mongolia, based out of Finland’s Embassy in Beijing (where he also serves as ambassador to China). Just weeks later, in January 2025, Mongolia’s non-resident ambassador to Finland – Munkh-Ulzii Tserendorj, who is based in Stockholm and also serves as ambassador to Sweden – presented his credentials to Stubb. Thus, Khurelsukh’s state visit and the strengthening of bilateral relations have been in the works for over a year. This was highlighted particularly during a bilateral meeting between Finnish Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen and Mongolian Foreign Minister Battsetseg Batmunkh in 2025.
Khurelsukh’s state visit to Helsinki encapsulated Ulaanbaatar’s interest in strengthening its links with Nordic countries as part of Mongolia’s third neighbor diversification strategy.

Following the one-on-one meeting between the two leaders, Mongolia and Finland signed 10 bilateral documents to strengthen cooperation in education, culture, museums, digital education, regional cooperation between Khuvsgul and Lappland, sustainable construction, and clean energy.

Senior diplomat Enkhmandakh Baldan, Mongolia’s first resident ambassador to Sweden and the Nordic region, was part of the Mongolian delegation. He stated that Mongolia can learn from the developmental models from all five Nordic countries: Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, and Sweden. Particularly, Mongolia can learn and adopt Finland’s equal education system, which has great influence on the Finnish society.

Khurelsukh visited the National Museum of Finland to view rare Mongolian relics, which are a crucial part of the historical and cultural ties between the two civilizations. The museum displays research work by linguist Gustaf John Ramstedt and archaeologist Sakari Palsi, who studied ancient inscriptions on stone monuments, as well as oral literature and music, during field visits to Mongolia in 1900 and 1909. As part of the expanding bilateral relations, Mongolia and Finland signed an agreement on museum cooperation.

The Mongolian delegation also paid their respects to the monument of Finnish General Baron Carl Gustaf Emil Mannerheim, a historical figure crucial to Finnish independence and sovereignty, also known as “Father of Finland.”
Moreover, the Finland Chamber of Commerce and the Mongolian National Chamber of Commerce and Industry organized the Finland-Mongolia Business Forum, with 70 business representatives from both sides.

Bilateral trade and business relations between Mongolia and Finland are modest, with trade amounting to just over $47 million in 2025. Nearly all of that came from Finland’s exports to Mongolia, including mining machinery and constructions equipment. Mongolia exported just $78,000 worth of goods to Finland last year.

“One of the objectives of President Khurelsukh’s visit was to strengthen trade between Finland and Mongolia,” the official readout from Finland’s presidential office said. Stubb expressed a desire to “expand our cooperation in areas such as mining and minerals, clean energy, education and digitalization.”

For its part, Mongolia aims to increase export of organic wools and cashmere items to Finland, as both countries share similar weather. Battsetseg told the press that Mongolia had proposed cooperation in energy efficient heating projects, agriculture, organic foods, wool and cashmere products. The Finnish side suggested cooperation in advanced technologies forestry, mining, wood processing, and winter tourism and sports.

In addition to cooperating in these sectors, Mongolia should not neglect Finland’s expertise in water resource management. The Scandinavian countries could help Mongolia address its chronic water security issues with robust technologies, but the impetus will need to come from Ulaanbaatar.

Finland’s anti-corruption system, sometimes credited to the adoption of the Law of Jante (Janteloven), is something else Mongolia ought to learn from. Finland has a track record of ranking in the top 3 in the Transparency International Corruption Perception Index (CPI), highlighting its leadership as a good governance model, particularly for small states.

In the realm of international relations, both Mongolia and Finland are considered “small states” and their foreign policy strategies rely heavily on diplomacy, strong commitment to democracy, multilateralism, stability, and rule-based international order. In practice, these shared values are instrumental foreign policy tools that can help both countries navigate geopolitical issues.
Mongolia and Finland’s geopolitical environment – both bordering Russia – is crucial in this context.

Russia’s invasion of Ukraine prompted Helsinki to abandon its longstanding neutrality policy and officially join NATO in 2023. Yet as a country neighboring Russia, Finland can’t afford to entirely cut Moscow off. Helsinki remains diplomatically engaged, as evidenced by Stubbs’ phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin on October 27.

Mongolia, situated in Northeast Asia where there is no regional security integration, must rely on historical, traditional, and diplomatic bilateral relations to navigate geopolitical issues and external threats. While there has been no significant shifts in Ulaanbaatar’s policy toward Russia, Mongolia has been impacted by war-related fuel shortages for months, and the country is expecting a rough winter.

In the last decade, both Mongolia and Finland’s core strategy on Asia has circled around diversifying economic partners in East Asia and Southeast Asia, with a particular focus on Singapore, another small state. Given Finland’s Asia strategy, strengthening bilateral relations with Mongolia aligns with Helsinki’s diversification strategy; the same is true for Ulaanbaatar.

As Mongolia and Finland prepare to celebrate their 65th anniversary of diplomatic relations in 2028, the high-level meeting between Stubb and Khurelsukh opened deeper cooperation mechanisms between two small states navigating a changing world.
